bottle.class: Blended Irish whiskey, labelled Irish whiskey
bottle.mash: Pot still whiskey from malted and unmalted Irish barley, married to grain whiskey; Difford's Guide gives the grain as corn and barley. The house publishes no shares in the blend.
bottle.still: Made at Midleton in County Cork: the pot still whiskey in copper pot stills, the grain whiskey in tall column stills, and, by the house's account, both distilled three times.

bottle.taste: By the house's notes, a light, floral nose with spicy wood and a gentle sweetness, then spice and toasted wood giving way to vanilla and nuts, a touch of sweet sherry, and a warm finish.

records.table: Pot still whiskey of malted and unmalted barley, married to light grain and triple distilled at Midleton in County Cork: that is Jameson Irish Whiskey. Vanilla, toasted wood and a hint of sherry come from bourbon and sherry casks; it is easy over ice or in an Irish Coffee.
records.story: John Jameson (1740 to 1823), a Scot from Alloa, came to Dublin and ran a distillery on Bow Street, and the house dates its beginning to 1780. Accounts differ on how he came to it: one says his wife's cousins, the Stein family, founded Bow Street and took him on as manager, and that he became its owner in 1805. John Jameson & Son was the firm's name by 1810. Through the twentieth century Irish whiskey lost much of its trade abroad, and in 1966 three firms, John Jameson & Son, John Power & Son and the Cork Distilleries Company, merged as Irish Distillers. Bow Street fell silent in the early 1970s, and the making moved to Midleton in County Cork, where a new distillery opened in 1975; in 1997 the Bow Street buildings opened as a visitor centre. Pot still for spice and body, grain for lightness: that is the plain lesson of an Irish blend, and Jameson, the Irish whiskey many guests ask for by name, teaches it.

records.story: The town of Tullamore in County Offaly gained a distillery in 1829. Daniel E. Williams (1848 to 1921) went to work at about fourteen in a Tullamore mill that soon became part of the distillery; he rose to run it as general manager, and his family later took the business over. His initials, D.E.W., gave the whiskey its name. In 1954 the old distillery closed, and for sixty years Tullamore D.E.W. was made elsewhere, for many years at Midleton in County Cork. William Grant & Sons bought the brand from C&C Group in 2010 and built a new distillery at Clonminch, on the edge of the town. It opened on 17 September 2014, and whiskey was made in Tullamore again for the first time in sixty years. Through every move the Original kept its shape: a blend of grain, malt and pot still whiskey. Jameson marries two Irish styles; the Original holds all three at once, and its light, easy character makes it a whiskey to reach for in a highball.

records.story: The house began with a bottled Irish Coffee, The Hot Irishman, which a husband and wife set out to make in County Carlow in 1999. Their company grew into Walsh Whiskey, blending and bottling whiskey from distilleries it did not own. The Irishman came next, and by the house's account Writers' Tears followed in 2009. As the house tells it, the name honours the Irish writers who sought inspiration and comfort in whiskey, and it calls on Yeats, Joyce and Beckett among them. The house also ties the marriage of pot still and malt to an Irish style of the nineteenth century that it calls the champagne of Irish whiskey. Walsh went into equal partnership with Illva Saronno, the Italian firm that makes Disaronno, and in 2016 the pair opened a distillery at Royal Oak, an estate in Carlow. They went separate ways in 2019, Illva keeping the distillery as Royal Oak Distillery and Walsh keeping Writers' Tears and The Irishman; Amber Beverage Group bought Walsh in 2021. The house names no distillery for the Copper Pot. The rule of thumb says a blend holds grain; Writers' Tears breaks it, for this Irish blend is pot still and malt alone.

records.table: Cork publicans ordered it by its salesman's first name, and the company put that name on the label: Paddy Irish Whiskey, a blend made at Midleton. Triple distilled, light, nutty and malty with a mellow finish, it is the Cork pour to set beside Jameson.
records.story: Four distilleries in the city of Cork joined in 1867 to form the Cork Distilleries Company, and the old distillery at Midleton came in the following year. The company's whiskey went out under a long name, Cork Distilleries Company Old Irish Whiskey. In the early 1880s it took on a young Cork salesman, and for nearly forty years, until he retired in 1921, he carried the whiskey round the pubs of the county, where publicans took to ordering it by his first name. In the early twentieth century, 1912 by one account and 1913 by the house's, the company put that name on the label: Paddy. In 1966 the Cork Distilleries Company joined John Jameson & Son and John Power & Son to form Irish Distillers, and the group gathered its making at the new Midleton distillery, opened in 1975. Irish Distillers sold the brand to the Sazerac Company of Louisiana in 2016 and agreed to go on making it at Midleton. Paddy is the Cork answer to Jameson: the same stills at Midleton, a lighter blend, and a name that came from the pubs.

records.story: Slane Castle stands above the River Boyne in County Meath, and since 1981 its grounds have held rock concerts, which helped keep the estate going. In 2009 the family began bottling Slane Castle Whiskey, a blend made for them at Cooley Distillery in County Louth, until Beam bought Cooley and, in 2012, stopped making whiskey for other labels. In 2015 Brown-Forman, the Kentucky company behind Jack Daniel's, bought Slane Castle Irish Whiskey and set about building a distillery in the castle's eighteenth-century stables and courtyards. The distillery opened in 2017, with three copper pot stills and six column stills. Slane Triple Casked came out in May of that year, blended at first from whiskey bought from other Irish distilleries, with the aim, as the house told it, of working the castle's own whiskey into the blend as it came of age. In 2026 Brown-Forman paused distilling at Slane, calling the pause temporary, while the visitor centre stayed open. Wood does the teaching in this blend: the same whiskeys rested in three kinds of cask, then married.

The family is described, not named. people.json gains Alex Conyngham and Henry Mountcharles, the two living forms the sources showed (a Spirits Business interview and a Wikipedia page).

The year field is the distillery's opening, 2017, in The Spirits Business and Fortune; Wikipedia's page on the castle's owner gives 2015, the year of the purchase. Accounts differ on whether distilling began in 2017 or March 2018, so the record gives no start of distilling.
The early Slane Castle Whiskey of 2009 was blended by Cooley's then blender, a living man already in people.json; he is not named. The fire that damaged the castle in 1991 is left out on one source.
One house page says the seasoned casks held Tennessee whiskey; the record says seasoned whiskey barrels, as the range pages do.

Added on 2026-11-23: Brown-Forman paused distilling at Slane in late May 2026, calling it a temporary change to its schedules, with the visitor centre kept open (The Spirits Business, Whisky Advocate, Food Dive, Just Drinks). Told as dated history; madeBy stays Slane Distillery, which blends and bottles the brand, and how long the pause lasts was not reported. Fortune gave way among the sources; the 2017 opening rests as before on The Spirits Business and Fortune.

changed: bottle.taste and table: the house's notes are vanilla, demerara sugar, ripe banana, caramel and butterscotch, then spice over dried fruit, and a finish of dried fruit and baking spice; now the house's, and the table's brown spice is baking spice.
bottle.still: the stills are told as built (three pot, six column, Difford's Guide), not as a present count; the first bottles is now the early bottles.
story: Beam bought Cooley in 2011 by one account; now Beam bought Cooley and in 2012 stopped making whiskey for others, as the Spirits Business brand history says.

story: Brown-Forman's first outside the United States cut: a claim of a first, which only Difford's Guide makes among the sources read, and it may be meant of a distillery built rather than one owned.
story: the stills made half the height to fit the protected buildings was in no source read; cut. Triple Casked came out in May 2017 (the Spirits Business).
others: Extra Sherry Wood is a release of the house's Wood Series, at first sold at airports and the distillery; the note says Wood Series.

story: one dated sentence added, Brown-Forman's pause of distilling at Slane in 2026, called temporary, with the visitor centre open (The Spirits Business, Whisky Advocate, Food Dive); sources: Fortune gave way to The Spirits Business on the pause; report notes it (label settler, 2026-11-23).
open: year: 2017 is the opening (public in August 2017); one trade piece gives 2016 for the purchase, the others 2015, which the record keeps.

bottle.mash: the distillery's own barley grain whiskey rests on Difford's Guide and the house's barley account; whether the blend now holds the castle's own whiskey is unsettled, and the record says neither. With distilling paused since 2026, the question now turns on stock already laid down.
